edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina 5 (1844), Arnobius, Disputationes adversus gentes, Liber I, via Latin Wikisource (Corpus Corporum TEI)
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Quoniam comperi nonnullos, qui se plurimum sapere suis persuasionibus credunt, insanire, bacchari, et velut quiddam promptum ex oraculo dicere: postquam esse in mundo christiana gens coepit, terrarum orbem periisse, multiformibus malis affectum esse genus humanum; ipsos etiam coelites, derelictis curis solemnibus, quibus quondam solebant invisere res nostras, terrarum ab regionibus exterminatos: statui pro captu, ac mediocritate sermonis contraire invidiae, et calumniosas dissolvere criminationes, ne aut illi sibi videantur, popularia dum verba depromunt, magnum aliquid dicere; aut, si nos talibus continuerimus a litibus, obtinuisse se causam putent, victam sui vitio, non assertorum silentio destitutam. Neque enim negaverim validissimam esse accusationem istam, hostilibusque condignos odiis nos esse, si apud nos esse constiterit causas, per quas suis mundus aberravit ab legibus, exterminati sunt dii longe, examina tanta moerorum mortalium importata sunt saeculis. Inspiciamus igitur opinionis istius mentem, et hoc quod dicitur, quale sit: summotisque omnibus contentionum studiis, quibus obscurari et contegi contemplatio rerum solet, an sit istud quod dicitur verum, momentorum parium examinatione pendamus. Efficietur enim profecto rationum consequentium copulatu, ut non impii nos magis, sed illi ipsi reperiantur criminis istius rei, qui se numinum profitentur esse cultores, atque inveteratis religionibus deditos. Ac primum ab his illud familiari et placida oratione perquirimus: postquam esse nomen in terris christianae religionis occoepit, quidnam invisitatum, quid incognitum, quid contra leges principaliter institutas, aut sensit aut passa est rerum ipsa quae dicitur appellaturque natura? Numquid in contrarias qualitates prima illa elementa mutata sunt, ex quibus res omnes consensum est esse concretas? Numquid machinae hujus, et molis, qua universi tegimur, et continemur inclusi, parte est in aliqua relaxata, aut dissoluta constructio? Numquid vertigo haec mundi, primigenii motus moderaren excedens, aut tardius repere, aut praecipiti coepit volubilitate raptari? Numquid ab occiduis partibus attolere se astra, atque in ortus fieri signorum coepta est inclinatio? Numquid ipse siderum sol princeps, cujus omnia luce vestiuntur, atque animantur calore, exarsit, intepuit, atque in contrarios habitus moderaminis soliti temperamenta corrupit? Numquid luna desivit redintegrare se ipsam, atque in veteres formas novellarum semper restitutione traducere? Numquid frigora, numquid calores, numquid tepores medii inaequalium temporum confusionibus occiderunt? Numquid longos habere dies bruma, revocare tardissimas luces nox coepit aestatis? Numquid suas animas expiraverunt venti? emortiusque flaminibus neque coelum coactatur in nubila, nec madidata ex imbribus arva succedunt? Commendata semina tellus recusat accidere, aut frondescere arbores nolunt? sapor frugibus esculentis, et vitis liquoribus mutatus est? olearum ex bacculis cruor teter exprimitur, nec lumini subministratur extincto? Animalia terris sueta, atque in aquis degentia non suriunt, nec concipiunt? foetus non in uteris sumptos suis moribus, et sua lege custodiunt? Ipsi homines denique, quos per inhabitabiles oras terrae sparsit prima incipiensque navitas, non matrimonia copulant nuptiarum solennibus justis? non dulcissimas procreant liberorum stirpes, non negotia publica, non privata, et familiares res agunt? non, ut cuique libitum est, per diversas artium, disciplinarumque rationes ingenia dirigunt, et studiosae referunt navitatis usuras? Non regnant, non imperant, quibus sors rerum attributa est talium? non auctiores quotidie dignitatibus et potestatibus fiunt? judiciorum disceptationibus praesunt? leges interpretantur et jura? Nonne omnia caetera, quibus vita succingitur et continetur humana, suis omnes in gentibus patriorum celebrant institutionibus morum?
pass_a_gloss: Since I have discovered that some people, who believe they know a great deal due to their own persuasions, are raving, being carried away, and as if something ready is being said from an oracle: after the Christian people began to exist in the world, the earth has perished, the human race has been affected by many evils; even the heavenly beings, having abandoned their solemn cares, with which they were once accustomed to visit our affairs, have been exterminated from the regions of the earth: I have decided, according to my ability and the mediocrity of my speech, to oppose envy and to dissolve calumnious accusations, so that neither do they seem to themselves to be saying something important while they utter popular words, nor, if we were to restrain ourselves from such disputes, do they think they have obtained their case, which has been conquered by its own fault, not by the silence of those who assert it. For I will not deny that this accusation is very strong and that we are worthy of hostile hatred, if it is established among us that there are causes by which the world has strayed from its laws, the gods have been exterminated, and so many mortal sorrows have been imported into the ages. Let us therefore examine the mind of this opinion and what is being said, and, having set aside all the contentious zeal with which the contemplation of things is usually obscured and covered, let us weigh whether what is being said is true by an examination of equal moments. For it will certainly be brought about by the connection of consequent reasons that not we, the impious, but they themselves will be found to be guilty of this crime, who claim to be cultivators of the divine and devoted to ancient religions. And first, we ask this from them in a familiar and peaceful speech: after the name of the Christian religion began to exist on earth, what unseen, what unknown, what contrary to the laws principally instituted has the nature of things itself, which is called and named, experienced or suffered? Have the first elements, from which all things are agreed to be composed, been changed into contrary qualities? Has any part of the machine and structure of the universe, with which we are covered and contained, been relaxed or dissolved? Has the rotation of the world, which moderates the original motion, begun to proceed more slowly or more quickly, or has it started to be carried away with a precipitous swiftness? Has the inclination of the stars to rise from the western parts and to become signs in the eastern parts begun? Has the sun, the prince of the stars, which clothes all things with its light and animates them with its heat, become inflamed, grown cold, and corrupted the temperaments of its usual moderation? Has the moon ceased to renew itself and to be led back into its old forms by the constant restitution of new things? Have the cold, the heat, and the moderate temperatures of unequal times perished in confusion? Has the winter begun to have long days and to recall the latest lights of the night in summer? Have the winds expired their breath? And have the flames died, so that the sky is not forced into clouds, nor do the fields, moistened by rains, follow? Does the earth refuse to receive the seeds that have been entrusted to it, or do the trees not want to sprout? Has the taste of edible fruits and the liquid of wines been changed? Does the blood of olives, expressed from their berries, not provide light when it is extinguished? Do the animals, which are accustomed to the earth and which live in the waters, not produce offspring, nor do they conceive? Do the fetuses not preserve their customs and their law in the wombs? Do men, finally, whom the first and beginning navigation has scattered over the uninhabitable shores of the earth, not join in marriages with the solemn rites of weddings? Do they not produce the most sweet offspring of children, not conduct public, not private, and not domestic affairs? Do they not, as it pleases each one, direct their talents through various arts and disciplines, and do they not repay the usuries of their studies? Do they not reign, do they not command, to whom the fate of such things has been attributed? Are they not becoming more powerful every day with dignities and powers? Do they not preside over judicial disputes? Do they not interpret laws and rights? Do not all other things, by which human life is sustained and contained, celebrate their institutions of customs in all nations?

choices.why: the Latin word 'bacchari' means to be carried away or to be in a state of frenzy
the Latin word 'oraculum' refers to a divine utterance or a prophetic statement
the Latin word 'coelites' refers to beings that inhabit the heavens or the sky
the Latin word 'invidia' refers to a feeling of ill will or resentment towards someone
the Latin word 'calumnia' refers to a false or malicious accusation

pass_b_english: I have discovered that certain people, convinced by their own reasoning that they possess superior wisdom, are in fact raving like fanatics and spouting pronouncements as if they came straight from an oracle. They claim that ever since the Christian religion appeared in the world, the earth has been ruined and the human race overwhelmed by every kind of misery. They even assert that the heavenly powers have abandoned their age-old duty of overseeing human affairs and have been driven from the regions of the earth. I have therefore decided, within the limits of my ability and my plain style, to confront this envy and dismantle these slanderous charges. I must act so that these accusers do not mistake their popular rhetoric for real substance, nor imagine that our silence would concede them a victory won by the weakness of their own case, not by any failure of its defenders.

I will not deny that their accusation carries great weight and that we deserve hostile hatred — if it can be proven that among us exist the causes that made the world stray from its laws, that exterminated the gods, and that imported such vast sorrows into the ages. Let us therefore examine the thinking behind this opinion and the actual claims being made. Setting aside all partisan zeal that usually obscures and buries the truth, let us weigh the evidence on balanced scales. A chain of rigorous reasoning will certainly show that the impious ones are not us, but the accusers themselves — those who boast of cultivating the divine and clinging to ancient rites.

First, I put this question to them in a calm and reasonable tone: since the name of the Christian religion began to exist on earth, what unseen disaster, what unknown cataclysm, what violation of the fundamental laws of nature has the world itself experienced or suffered? Have the primary elements, from which all things are composed, been transmuted into opposite qualities? Has any part of the cosmic machine that envelops and contains us been loosened or dissolved? Has the world's rotation, which governs the primal motion, begun to drag or to race, or has it been seized by a headlong, precipitous speed? Have the stars started rising in the west and setting in the east? Has the sun, the prince of the stars, which clothes all things in light and animates them with heat, flared up or gone cold, corrupting the balanced temperaments of its usual course? Has the moon ceased to renew itself and return to its ancient phases through the constant cycle of waxing and waning? Have cold, heat, and the moderate temperatures of the irregular seasons perished in confusion? Has winter begun to stretch its days long and summer nights to recall the latest dawns? Have the winds breathed their last? Have the lightning flashes died out, so that the sky no longer condenses into clouds and rain-moistened fields no longer follow? Does the earth refuse the seed committed to it? Do trees refuse to put forth leaves? Have the flavor of edible fruits and the juice of the vine been altered? Does the oil pressed from olives no longer feed lamps when they go out? Do land animals and sea creatures no longer breed or conceive? Do fetuses no longer develop in the womb according to their nature and law? Finally, do human beings — scattered by the first seafaring to the world's uninhabitable shores — no longer join in marriage with solemn rites? Do they no longer beget children, conduct public and private business, or manage their households? Do they no longer direct their talents through diverse arts and disciplines as they please, and reap the returns of their labors? Do those to whom the lot of rule has fallen no longer reign or command? Are they not daily growing greater in dignity and power? Do they not preside over courts, interpret laws, and administer justice? Do not all the other institutions that sustain and structure human life continue to be observed in every nation according to ancestral custom?

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the rhetorical questions and the complex structure of the Latin text. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the source. All clauses, including the long list of natural phenomena and human social structures, are accounted for. No omissions or misinterpretations of agency or modality were found.
